questions.q: The correct order of electrophilic substitution for the compounds given above will be
questions.solution:
An electron releasing group stablilises the carbocation by dispersing its positive charge and thus activates the ring while an electron-withdrawing group destabilises the carbocation by intensifying its positive charge and thus deactivates the ring. $-\mathrm{NH}_{2}$ being electron releasing group releases electron and thus tend to neutralise positive charge of the ring and itself becomes somewhat positive. The dispersal of positive charge of the ring stabilises carbocation and hence facilitates its formation which ultimately results an increased rate of reaction. Now since such factor is not present in benzene, its carbocation is less stable than (A). Hence aniline undergoes electrophilic substitution at a faster rate than benzene.
On the other hand in $(\mathrm{C})$ the $-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ group (an electron withdrawing group) intensifies positive charge on the ring and thus destabilises the carbocation and hence its formation becomes difficult which ultimately results a slower reaction. Now since substituent is not present in benzene, its carbocation (B) is relatively more stable than (C). Hence nitrobenzene undergoes electrophilic substitution at a slower rate than benzene.

questions.q: What is the area of a loop of the curve $\mathrm{r}=\operatorname{asin} 3 \theta$ ?
questions.solution:
If curve $\mathrm{r}=\mathrm{a} \sin 3 \theta$ To trace the curve, we consider the following table : \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline 3 \theta= & 0 & \frac{\pi}{2} & \pi & \frac{3 \pi}{2} & 2 \pi & \frac{5 \pi}{2} & 3 \pi \\ \hline\theta= & 0 & \frac{\pi}{6} & \frac{\pi}{3} & \frac{\pi}{2} & \frac{2 \pi}{3} & \frac{5 \pi}{6} & \pi \\ \hline \mathrm{r}= & 0 & \mathrm{a} & 0 & -\mathrm{a} & 0 & \mathrm{a} & 0 \\ \hline \end{array} Thus there is a loop between $\theta=0 \& \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$ as r varies from $\mathrm{r}=0$ to $\mathrm{r}=0$.
Hence, the area of the loop lying in the \text { positive quadrant }=\frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} r^{2} \mathrm{~d} \theta =\frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \sin ^{2} \phi \cdot \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~d} \phi $\left[\right.$ On putting, $\left.3 \theta=\phi \Rightarrow \mathrm{d} \theta=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~d} \phi\right]$ \begin{array}{c} =\frac{a^{2}}{6} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin ^{2} \phi \mathrm{d} \phi \\ =\frac{\mathrm{a}^{2}}{6} \cdot \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{1-\cos 2 \phi}{2} \mathrm{~d} \phi\left[\because \cos 2 \theta=1-2 \sin ^{2} \theta\right] \end{array} $=\frac{\mathrm{a}^{2}}{12} \cdot\left[\phi+\frac{\sin 2 \phi}{2}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}=\frac{\mathrm{a}^{2}}{12} \cdot\left[\frac{\pi}{2}+\sin \pi\right]=\frac{\mathrm{a}^{2} \pi}{24}$

questions.q: For what value of $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{C}$, the output $\mathrm{Y}=1$
questions.solution:
Clearly,

\mathrm{Y}=(\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B}) \cdot \mathrm{C}=(\mathrm{A} \cdot \mathrm{C})+(\mathrm{B} \cdot \mathrm{C})

For

\begin{array}{ll}
\mathrm{A}=0, \mathrm{~B}=0 \& \mathrm{C}=1, & \mathrm{Y}=(0.1)+(0.1)=0 \\
\mathrm{~A}=1, \mathrm{~B}=0 \& \mathrm{C}=1, & \mathrm{Y}=(1.1)+(0.1)=1 \\
\mathrm{~A}=1, \mathrm{~B}=0 \& \mathrm{C}=0, & \mathrm{Y}=(0.1)+(0.0)=0 \\
\mathrm{~A}=0, \mathrm{~B}=1 \& \mathrm{C}=0, & \mathrm{Y}=(0.0)+(1.0)=0
\end{array}

So, option (b) is correct.

questions.q: A metallic bar is heated from $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. The coeficient of linear expansion is $10^{-5} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$. What will be the percentage increase in length?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}
\frac{\Delta \ell}{\ell}=\alpha \Delta \mathrm{T} &=10^{-5} \times 100=10^{-3} \\
\frac{\Delta \ell}{\ell} \times 100 \% &=10^{-3} \times 100 \\
&=10^{-1}=0.1 \%
\end{aligned}$
